name: Ivan Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and run a board edge-banding machine for cupboard panels. My vocational certificate taught glue temperature and safe stops. I like a clean, smooth edge; scraping a jammed glue pot after the line cools is slow and sticky.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner delivers school meals. We have two school-age children, a mortgage and about ten months of expenses saved. My board-line rate is higher than usual for this job, and plenty of similar workshops are nearby. I never use AI tools; I take a doubtful temperature reading to the setter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the board shop an office tool may type the cutting schedule, but it will not feel a loose edge strip on a cupboard panel. We still need someone at the edge-banding machine. I would not make a speech about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The board-line rate is above the usual machine pay, and my partner earns a steady wage delivering school meals. We have about ten months of expenses saved, a mortgage and two school-age children. Plenty of similar workshops are nearby, so I feel sound at present.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep setting the edge-bander, trimming the glued strip and checking the first panel of each run. I never use AI and will ask the setter directly if a temperature reading looks wrong. I'll take the offered Saturday work if a large kitchen order comes through, mostly because I like keeping the line tidy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The mortgage is covered and the work makes sense to me. I can see a bad edge before anyone has to argue with a computer about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a weak glued edge look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On a cupboard door, a cold glue line leaves a strip that peels near the corner. I run my thumb across the cooled edge and stop the next panel if it lifts. A cupboard door should not arrive with its edge already peeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do your wages fit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner's school-meal route is regular, though it pays less than the board line. We keep the ten-month reserve for a real gap or a house repair. The children know we fix broken things before replacing them.

Our **edge-banding line** still needs first-panel checks by an operator.
think: My **higher board wage** and ten-month reserve support the mortgage.
My partner’s **school-meal route** is steady, and nearby workshops offer options.
do: **Keep** setting the edge-bander and checking first cupboard panels before each full production run.
**Ask** the setter directly about unusual glue temperatures.
feel: **Calm** about current paid work and household money.
S0.quote: A cupboard door should not arrive with its edge already peeling.
fieldNote: Ivan **never uses AI** and trusts cooled-edge checks plus a familiar setter.
The **higher rate**, regular second wage, ten-month reserve and many workshops support his calm baseline.

steps.text: Keep setting edge-bander and checking first cupboard panels

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI may order boards and plan sizes before robots can feed them through the bander. Management should post the new paid roster before promising faster delivery. I would check the actual waste pile, not only a slide with percentages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A planning tool might squeeze our changeover time and take a few paid hours from me. Ten months saved helps, but the high board-line rate is worth protecting because my partner's school-meal wage would not replace it. I can find other workshops, yet their rates may be lower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the supervisor for the posted base-hours rota and compare it with last month's slips. I'll keep checking the first panel at each changeover. If the factory requires a new guard-setting course and offers it on paid time with a trainer at a stopped bander, I'll attend; I won't spend evenings learning a private AI app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about paid hours, though I can wait for a real rota. A lost high-rate shift still leaves a hole even when there is money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would guard training need to teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trainer should make me isolate the glue pot, check the guard switch and feed a scrap board after restart. I would practise on a stopped line first. Watching somebody else do it will not tell me what my hands should touch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which pay figure would you compare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want the base shifts, because overtime changes every month. If the new rota cuts a full day, I would compare the missing pay with the school-meal wage and mortgage. A nearby board-line job is only useful if its base rate covers the mortgage gap.

Management should show a **paid roster** and real waste checks before faster targets.
think: A shorter **changeover rota** could reduce my high-rate hours.
Ten months saved gives time, but **nearby wages** may not match.
do: **Compare** posted base shifts with actual pay slips.

**Attend** required paid guard-setting course if a trainer-led stopped-line place is offered.
feel: **Anxious** about a realistic cut to higher-paid hours.
S1.quote: A nearby board-line job is only useful if its base rate covers the mortgage gap.
fieldNote: His **risk avoidance** leads to real rota checks before accepting a new target.
Required **hands-on training** is conditional on paid time, a trainer and a stopped guarded bander.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the shop thinking AI could plan cupboard orders by 2028, and capable robots around 2031 could feed, trim and inspect the board line. I would ask the owner for the machine date and the paid jobs left. I do not want a rumour doing the owner's work for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when the physical robots arrive. The higher edge-banding wage might go even if I can find another factory, and the mortgage still needs a regular pay packet. Ten months saved and plenty of nearby workshops give us a search window, but no one has offered me the same rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the owner for a written staffing and pay plan now. If the company offers funded paid-time practical training in machine inspection on a locked bander, I'll take a real place. If my hours fall, I'll apply to posted safe local board-line jobs with base wages and shifts that cover our bills and school pickup; once qualified, I'll also apply for posted local inspection roles under the same terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing a better wage, but I can make calls and compare offers. I would not leave my paying edge-banding line for a promised inspection post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would practical inspection involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want a training load with a peeling edge, a stopped glue pot and a supervisor watching the check. The inspection skill is judging the cooled board and knowing when to stop the line. A certificate without those hours would not persuade me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What vacancy would you try first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first vacancy I would consider is a posted board-line role within a workable school trip. I would ask for the base rate, paid hours and guard rules before applying. If it pays far less than our bills need, I keep looking.

say: **2028 thinking AI** could plan orders before robots handle boards around 2031.
The owner should publish a **staffing date** and remaining paid jobs.
think: At **48**, I could lose a higher edge-banding wage.
Ten months saved and **many workshops** permit a search without guaranteeing equal pay.
do: **Ask** owner for written staffing and pay terms.
**Attend** funded paid locked-line inspection training if a place is offered.
**Apply** to posted safe local board or qualified inspection if cut, pay and school trips fit.
feel: **Anxious** about potential loss of the higher wage with several options.
S2.quote: I would not leave my paying edge-banding line for a promised inspection post.
fieldNote: He treats **local job abundance** as search options, not a guarantee of matching his high rate.
The **board fallback** and qualified inspection application need real posted safe roles, adequate base pay and school-compatible hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI could plan board orders in 2031 and capable robots might work the bander around 2034. Five years gives us time to learn whether the plant actually needs inspectors. I would ask for a paid course and a posted job, separately.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 51 when robots can handle the boards. Our two children will be older, and I expect the mortgage still to need wages. I could pay down more of it while high-rate shifts last, but I would not buy a course before seeing an offered place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the bander job and pay extra mortgage principal from any offered full-rate overtime after bills. I'll ask the plant for a funded paid-time quality certificate with guarded practice and a real seat; if offered, I'll enrol. After qualifying, if board hours fall, I'll apply for posted safe local quality jobs only if their base pay and travel let us cover the mortgage and family schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a future drop in my wage, but the longer warning lets me ask one question at a time. The bank does not accept a course catalogue as a payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a quality certificate test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would measure a peeling edge after the board cools, then check the glue temperature and record a rejected batch. Someone qualified needs to watch me isolate the line. A course without that practice would not make me an inspector.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the quality post pays less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The posting needs its base wage and travel days in writing. If it is a lower-rate job an hour away, the mortgage and school trips may not fit. I would keep the current paid shift while I looked elsewhere.

The plant should offer **paid quality training** and a separate real posted job.
think: At **51**, the mortgage may still need my wage.
Full-rate overtime could support **extra principal payments** if shifts are offered.
do: **Pay** extra mortgage principal from offered full-rate overtime after bills.
**Enrol** in quality training if funded paid guarded seat offered.
**Apply** for posted safe local quality if qualified, hours fall, base pay and travel fit.
feel: **Anxious** about future loss of a high-rate wage.
S3.quote: The bank does not accept a course catalogue as a payment.
fieldNote: His **new debt payment** comes from offered overtime wages, while current ten-month savings remain available.
The **quality application** follows actual qualification and hour loss, with a posted safe local role at sufficient pay and workable travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI might plan board orders in 2036 and capable robots around 2039 might feed the bander. Ten years lets us ask for proof before making a move. I would tell the family what the posted wages say, not what a salesman says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 56 when physical robots arrive. Our children may be grown, but the mortgage could still need my higher operator pay. Ten months saved gives us time to choose and many local board plants give possible openings if their rates hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the bander shift and use newly earned full-rate overtime to pay extra mortgage principal after bills. I'll ask my brother, who repairs timber machines, which nearby firms offer real paid guarded apprenticeships. If a funded paid place with a trainer is offered, I'll enrol; if my board hours later shrink, I'll apply after qualifying to posted safe local repair jobs only if the base wage and travel work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about a far-off line change, while our current wages are sound. I can wait for an offered place without closing my eyes to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What can your brother find out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother can tell me what a repair apprentice actually earns and whether a shop locks its machine before teaching. My brother who repairs timber machines cannot reserve an apprenticeship seat for me. I would check the posted fee, wages and hours with the employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge a repair posting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the base wage with the mortgage and the time home with the children's needs. A longer trip for a smaller wage would not suit us. I would stay on the bander while I checked other posted jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case worries me most because capable robots around 2031 could cut the high-rate edge-banding hours that support our mortgage. A written staffing plan, offered paid guarded practical training and posted safe local work at a dependable base rate would help. I would compare the shift with school needs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks a cupboard door after a robot glues its edge. A peeling edge makes a cupboard look old before anyone has used it.

headlineQuote: A peeling edge makes a cupboard look old before anyone has used it.
portrait: **Ivan**, 43, runs a cupboard-board edge-bander with a vocational certificate, higher pay and ten months saved.
He and his school-meal-driver partner support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage, with plentiful local workshops.
His **centre outlook** favors posted wages and real rosters; he never uses AI and prefers familiar hands-on teaching.
Fast robots make him **anxious** about losing the higher rate, while the reserve and local jobs permit a careful search.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring capable board-line robots around 2031 and cut his higher-paid shifts.
whatWouldHelp: A **written staffing plan**, offered paid guarded training and posted safe local work at sufficient base pay would help.
